title: My God, why (Psalm 21 [22])
hook: the psalm Jesus prayed from the cross, which ends in praise

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heavens shew forth: a sky that speaks without words. Your line was the sky is preaching. Did you look up three times? Today, a psalm from the dark. Day one hundred sixty-two.

Good Friday, the ninth hour. Jesus has been on the cross since morning. The sky has gone dark. And then, the Gospels say, he cries out with a loud voice, in his own language, words that bystanders mishear. Matthew writes them down: "Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani? that is, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" For two thousand years, people have stopped at that sentence. It sounds like the bottom of the world. But anyone standing there who knew the psalms would have recognized it. He wasn't inventing those words. He was praying them.
screen: `THE NINTH HOUR.` → `MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY?` → `HE WAS PRAYING A PSALM.`

segments.voice: They're the first line of Psalm 21 in the Douay, 22 in most Bibles. In the Douay-Rheims: "O God my God, look upon me: why hast thou forsaken me?" In the ancient world, you often named a psalm by its first line, the way we'd name a song by its opening words. So when Jesus cries that line, many readers hear him calling up the whole psalm. And the whole psalm is astonishing. The first half is as dark as scripture gets. The one praying is mocked; people shake their heads and say, let God rescue him, then. He's poured out like water, his bones out of joint, his heart like melting wax, his tongue stuck to his jaw. "They parted my garments amongst them; and upon my vesture they cast lots." The Gospels tell that very thing happening at the foot of the cross, and John quotes the line. Then, near the end, the psalm turns. It stops asking why and starts thanking. God has not despised the poor man's cry. The poor will eat and be filled. All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and people not yet born will be told what God has done. It begins in abandonment and ends with the whole world praising. How to understand Jesus praying this is something Christians have thought about for centuries. The Church has held both things at once: that he truly felt the full weight of that cry, and that he prayed it as a psalm of trust whose ending he knew. Either way, the words were given to anyone who has ever felt forsaken. Even this is prayer.
screen: `A PSALM NAMED BY ITS FIRST LINE.` · `MOCKED, POURED OUT LIKE WATER.` · `THEY CAST LOTS FOR HIS VESTURE.` · `IT ENDS IN PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the first line for someone in pain. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who feels abandoned right now: grieving, sick, lonely, far from home, far from God. Don't try to fix it. Just stand next to them in your mind. If you pray, you can say the psalm's first line on their behalf, the way Jesus did: my God, my God, why? Say it honestly, and let it be a prayer. If you don't, simply hold them in your attention. The bell holds the time.
My God. The cry that opens Psalm 21, prayed by Jesus from the cross, from a psalm that begins forsaken and ends in praise. Today's word.
Your line: even this is prayer. Today, if a why rises up in you, don't swallow it. Say it, and count it as prayer. Day one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Psalm 21 [22] as the responsorial psalm on Palm Sunday, just before the Passion is read, and pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours; many pray its first line in times of desolation.

original.note: Hebrew: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? the Gospels give it in Aramaic form, sabachthani.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus's cry of despair.
what it means: the first line of a psalm that begins forsaken and ends in praise, prayed from the cross.
what a scholar hears: Matthew and Mark give the cry in Aramaic form (sabachthani, not the Hebrew azavtani), and bystanders mishear Eli as a call to Elijah.

notes: Douay wording of Matthew 27:46 and Psalm 21:2, 21:19: confirm against a Challoner edition.

CCC 603: Jesus, in his love, assumed us in the state of our estrangement so that he could say in our name, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' The script's 'both at once' summary is a paraphrase of a range of Catholic readings; a Keeper should check the balance.
The idea that citing a psalm's first line evokes the whole psalm is a common interpretation, hedged 'many readers'.
Aramaic form in Mark (Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani) and Matthew (Eli, Eli); bystanders think he calls Elijah. Confirm.
Palm Sunday responsorial psalm is Psalm 22 [21] in all three years. Confirm.
